content: 1. Ellen (2013) provided data exclusively for the intervention group, with no equivalent data available for the comparison group regarding the uptake of social network approaches (SNA). 2. Ellen (2012) utilized a purposively selected, non-randomized comparison group. 3. The study by Ellen (2013) was downgraded twice due to a lack of control for potential confounding factors and a small sample size, which posed a significant risk of bias. 4. The inconsistency of findings could not be assessed as the evidence was derived from a single study with a limited sample size. 5. Baytop (2014) evaluated the effectiveness of three strategies for reaching and motivating previously undiagnosed African American men who have sex with men (MSM). 6. Guo (2011) examined differences in HIV infection rates among migrant MSM in China recruited using four different sampling methods. 7. Halkitis (2011) conducted a prospective study to evaluate the effectiveness of three HIV testing strategies: social network strategies, alternate venue testing, and partner counseling and referral services. 8. Clark (2014) compared three recruitment methods—convenience sampling (CS), time-space sampling (TSS), and respondent-driven sampling (RDS)—for MSM and transgender women. 9. Studies by Smyrnov (2018), Katz (2016), Kan (2018), and Lightfoot (2018) were excluded from the meta-analysis due to differences in comparison groups. 10. Baytop (2014), Clark (2014), Guo (2011), and Halkitis (2011) were prospective cohort studies. 11. These studies were downgraded twice due to insufficient information on handling missing data in Baytop, Halkitis, and Clark, as well as serious concerns about potential confounding in Guo. 12. Some studies, such as Baytop and Halkitis, presented outcome data for only a subset of participants, such as contacts without prior HIV diagnoses or those tested for HIV. 13. Variability in outcomes could be attributed to differences in populations (e.g., MSM, transgender individuals, people who inject drugs), geographic locations (e.g., USA, Peru, China), and outcome definitions and measurements. 14. Baytop reported HIV positivity among contacts without prior HIV diagnoses who were tested for HIV, while Clark reported HIV positivity among all participants. Guo reported HIV positivity among all contacts, and Halkitis reported HIV positivity among contacts tested for HIV. 15. The exact cause of heterogeneity could not be determined from a single subgroup, leading to a downgrade in evidence quality. 16. Linjongrat (2018) conducted a non-comparative study in Thailand. 17. The ROBINS-I assessment could not determine the risk of bias for Linjongrat (2018) due to insufficient information on how each domain was handled, resulting in a classification of Not enough information. 18. Carballo-Dieguez (2012) reported on the use of SNA approaches for distributing HIV self-test kits among MSM in the USA. 19. Thirumurthy (2016) reported on the use of SNA approaches for distributing HIV self-test kits among female sex workers (FSW) in Kenya. 20. Thirumurthy (2016) identified a serious risk of bias due to self-reported outcomes, missing data, and a lack of control for potential confounding factors. 21. Studies showed similar outcome definitions and measurements, such as social harms or adverse events among index clients. 22. Carballo-Dieguez (2012) reported five instances of verbal arguments as social harms, with no physical violence. 23. Thirumurthy (2016) reported two cases of physical violence among sex workers in Kenya. 24. The authors noted a high prevalence of background intimate partner violence (IPV) in the study sample, with 41% reporting IPV.
